1. Write a professional customer email (responding to a complaint)

## Audit report: *Extending the Córdoba–Martínez-Zoroa IPM Blow-Up to Uniformly Space-Time Smooth Forcing*

**Source inspected:** `<HOME>/Downloads/ipm.pdf` and the extracted text `ipm.txt`. The PDF is 57 pages, dated September 7, 2026. I did not independently reprove or formally verify the argument.

### 1. Exact theorem and claimed result

The central statement is **Theorem 2.1, p. 3**, with the construction completed in **Section 6, pp. 42–48**.

For the forced periodic incompressible porous media equation
\[
\partial_t\rho+u_T(\rho)\cdot\nabla\rho=F
\quad\text{on }[0,1)\times\mathbb T^2,
\]
the paper claims existence of:

- smooth, odd, zero-mean initial data \(\rho_{\rm in}\in C^\infty(\mathbb T^2)\);
- a smooth, odd, zero-mean force
  \[
  F\in C^\infty([0,1]\times\mathbb T^2);
  \]
- a solution satisfying
  \[
  \rho\in C^\infty([0,T]\times\mathbb T^2)
  \quad\text{for every }T<1;
  \]
- a limiting density \(\rho_*\in C^\eta(\mathbb T^2)\) for every \(0\leq\eta<1\), with
  \[
  \rho(t)\to\rho_*\quad\text{in }C^\eta\text{ as }t\uparrow1;
  \]
- but nevertheless
  \[
  \|\nabla\rho(t)\|_{L^\infty}\to\infty,
  \qquad
  \|D_xu_T(\rho(t))\|_{L^\infty}\to\infty.
  \]

Thus the claimed singularity is loss of Lipschitz/\(C^1\) control at finite time, while the density remains bounded and converges in every sub-Lipschitz Hölder space.

109|### 5. Relation to Navier–Stokes and singularity questions

32|## Construction mechanism
33|
34|The construction is a deliberately engineered, forced Euler solution:
35|
36|1. Rewrite axisymmetric Euler with swirl in volume coordinates \(y=(z,r^2/2)\), using circulation \(\Gamma\), streamfunction \(\Psi\), reduced vorticity \(\xi\), and a variable elliptic operator (Section 2, pp. 3–7).
37|2. Start from a compactly supported rotating base field.
38|3. Add successive localized oscillatory “layers” at increasing frequencies \(N_m\) and decreasing spatial scales.
39|4. Transport each new oscillation by the exact nonlinear flow generated by all preceding fields, rather than by a fixed affine background (Sections 3–5, pp. 7–23).

41|6. Use phase inversion and finite correction equations to cancel nonzero oscillatory residuals. The remaining residuals are converted into the physical force through a fixed compactly supported curl inverse (Sections 5–6, pp. 15–27).
42|7. After each growth phase, choose a return time at which the principal azimuthal-vorticity amplitude and a covector component vanish. This resets the principal vorticity component while preserving the amplified circulation gradient and prepares the next layer (Propositions 4.2 and 7.6–7.7, pp. 14–37).
43|8. Choose one infinite causal sequence of layers whose insertion times converge to finite \(T_*\). The force increments satisfy summable bounds such as
44|   \[
45|   \|f_m\|_{C^k_{x,t}}\lesssim N_m^{-1/2}
46|   \]
47|   for sufficiently large layer order, so the force extends smoothly through \(T_*\) (Proposition 12.3, pp. 104–105; Lemma 13.2, pp. 107–108).

## Audit report: *Extending the Córdoba–Martínez-Zoroa IPM Blow-Up to Uniformly Space-Time Smooth Forcing*

**Source inspected:** `<HOME>/Downloads/ipm.pdf` and the extracted text `ipm.txt`. The PDF is 57 pages, dated September 7, 2026. I did not independently reprove or formally verify the argument.

### 1. Exact theorem and claimed result

The central statement is **Theorem 2.1, p. 3**, with the construction completed in **Section 6, pp. 42–48**.

For the forced periodic incompressible porous media equation
\[
\partial_t\rho+u_T(\rho)\cdot\nabla\rho=F
\quad\text{on }[0,1)\times\mathbb T^2,
\]
the paper claims existence of:

- smooth, odd, zero-mean initial data \(\rho_{\rm in}\in C^\infty(\mathbb T^2)\);
- a smooth, odd, zero-mean force
  \[
  F\in C^\infty([0,1]\times\mathbb T^2);
  \]
- a solution satisfying
  \[
  \rho\in C^\infty([0,T]\times\mathbb T^2)
  \quad\text{for every }T<1;
  \]
- a limiting density \(\rho_*\in C^\eta(\mathbb T^2)\) for every \(0\leq\eta<1\), with
  \[
  \rho(t)\to\rho_*\quad\text{in }C^\eta\text{ as }t\uparrow1;
  \]
- but nevertheless
  \[

Suppose that you are organizing housing accommodations for a group of four hundred university students. Space is limited and only one hundred of the students will receive places in the dormitory. To complicate matters, the Dean has provided you with a list of pairs of incompatible students, and requested that no pair from this list appear in your final choice. This is an example of what computer scientists call an NP-problem, since it is easy to check if a given choice of one hundred students proposed by a coworker is satisfactory (i.e., no pair taken from your coworker’s list also appears on the list from the Dean’s office), however the task of generating such a list from scratch seems to be so hard as to be completely impractical. Indeed, the total number of ways of choosing one hundred students from the four hundred applicants is greater than the number of atoms in the known universe! Thus no future civilization could ever hope to build a supercomputer capable of solving the problem by brute force; that is, by checking every possible combination of 100 students. However, this apparent difficulty may only reflect the lack of ingenuity of your programmer. In fact, one of the outstanding problems in computer science is determining whether questions exist whose answer can be quickly checked, but which require an impossibly long time to solve by any direct procedure. The standard computer model in computability theory is the Turing machine, introduced by Alan Turing in 1936 [37]. 2. History and Importance

The importance of the P vs NP question stems from the successful theories of NP-completeness and complexity-based cryptography, as well as the potentially stunning practical consequences of a constructive proof of P = NP. The theory of NP-completeness has its roots in computability theory, which originated in the work of Turing, Church, G¨odel, and others in the 1930s. The computability precursors of the classes P and NP are the classes of decidable and c.e. (computably enumerable) languages, respectively. We say that a language L is c.e. Of central importance in computability theory is the notion of reducibility, which Turing defined roughly as follows: A language L1 is Turing reducible to a language L2 iff there is an oracle Turing machine M that accepts L1, where M is allowed to make membership queries of the form x ∈ L2, which are correctly answered by an “oracle” for L2. Later, the more restricted notion of many-one reducibility (≤ m) was introduced and defined as follows. Definition 1. Suppose that Li is a language over Σi, i = 1, 2. Since ≤ m is transitive, to show that a c.e. language L is c.e.-complete it suffices to show that HP ≤ m L. The notion of polynomial-time computation was introduced in the 1960s by Cob ham [8] and Edmonds [13] as part of the early development of computational com plexity theory (although earlier von Neumann [38], in 1953, distinguished between polynomial-time and exponential-time algorithms). Edmonds called polynomial time algorithms “good algorithms” and linked them to tractable algorithms. It has now become standard in complexity theory to identify polynomial-time with feasible, and here we digress to discuss this point. It is of course not literally true that every polynomial-time algorithm can be feasibly executed on small inputs; for example, a computer program requiring n 100 steps could never be executed on an input even as small as n = 10. Here is a more defensible statement (see [10]): Feasibility Thesis. A natural problem has a feasible algorithm iff it has a poly nomial-time algorithm. Examples of natural problems that have both feasible and polynomial-time al gorithms abound: Integer arithmetic, linear algebra, network flow, linear program ming, many graph problems (connectivity, shortest path, minimum spanning tree, bipartite matching), etc. On the other hand, the deep results of Robertson and Seymour [29] provide a potential source of counterexamples to the thesis: They

However, each potential counterex ample can be removed by finding a feasible algorithm for it. For example, a feasible recognition algorithm is known for the class of planar graphs, but none is currently known for the class of graphs embeddable in R 3 with no two cycles linked. It distinguishes the formal complexity class from the operational cost of solving, validating, transporting, reproducing, and repeatedly revalidating solutions inside a containing network.\\n\\n## 1. What the Clay statement actually says\\n\\nStephen Cook\u2019s Clay statement defines:\\n\\n- P as languages accepted by a deterministic Turing machine whose worst-case runtime T_M(n) is bounded by a fixed polynomial in input length n.\\n- NP as languages L for which there is a polynomial-time checking relation R(w,y), and a polynomially bounded certificate y, such that w is in L exactly when some such y makes R(w,y) true.\\n- The problem as: Does P = NP?\\n\\nThe associated search problem is: given w, find a certificate y satisfying R(w,y), or determine that w is a NO instance. Cook notes that an efficient decision procedure can be used to construct a certificate through repeated queries.\\n\\nThe official source is:\\nhttps://www.claymath.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/pvsnp.pdf\\n\\nThe popular Clay explanation compresses this to: if it is easy to check that a solution is correct, is it also easy to solve the problem?\\n\\nThat compression is useful, but incomplete. \u201cEasy\u201d means polynomial in the formal input/certificate lengths under the selected computational model. It does not mean cheap in electricity, organizational effort, network latency, human review, or total lifecycle cost.\\n\\n## 2. The strongest version of the user\u2019s insight\\n\\nA problem is not operationally solved once. It passes through a lifecycle:\\n\\n```text\\nproblem specification\\n  -> encoding and decomposition\\n  -> candidate generation\\n  -> certificate/proof construction\\n  -> validation\\n  -> transport and integration\\n  -> reproduction\\n  -> revalidation under changed context\\n  -> deployment or decision\\n```\\n\\nEach stage has a cost. A proof that is mathematically valid but cannot be reconstructed, transported, audited, or updated may be a solution in the abstract and an expensive failure in the system that needs to use it.\\n\\nThis yields a more precise thesis:\\n\\n> Standard P and NP classify a language relative to an abstract machine and a certificate relation. Operational difficulty classifies a problem relative to a system architecture: its solver, verifier, communication graph, memory, interfaces, failure modes, and revalidation obligations.\\n\\nThis is an extension of the cost model, not a refutation of the formal classes.\\n\\n## 3. The network architecture variables\\n\\nLet a problem instance be x, with abstract language L and certificate relation R.\\n\\nLet A be a solving architecture. A may include:\\n\\n- compute nodes and their local computational models;\\n- communication graph G and edge latency/bandwidth;\\n- shared or replicated memory;\\n- decomposition and orchestration policy;\\n- solver family S;\\n- verifier family V;\\n- certificate format and provenance requirements;\\n- trust assumptions and failure/recovery rules;\\n- human or institutional review steps;\\n- versioning and revalidation policy.\\n\\nThen distinguish at least six costs:\\n\\n1. Solve cost: C_solve(A,x), including search, decomposition, retries, and coordination.\\n2. Validate cost: C_validate(A,x,y), including checking R(x,y), proof parsing, dependency resolution, and reviewer effort.\\n3. Transport cost: C_transport(A,y), including moving the certificate and required context across the network.\\n4. Reproduce cost: C_reproduce(A,x,y), for an independent node rebuilding the result.\\n5. Revalidation cost: C_revalidate(A,x,y,t), when software, data, assumptions, or surrounding claims change.\\n6. Failure cost: C_failure(A), expected cost of undetected errors, disagreement, stale artifacts, or Byzantine participants.\\n\\nA practical total cost is not merely runtime:\\n\\nC_total = C_solve + C_validate + C_transport + C_reproduce + C_revalidate + C_failure.\\n\\nThe terms need declared units. \u201cCheap\u201d may mean machine steps, dollars, joules, wall-clock time, human minutes, or risk-adjusted cost. Without that declaration, the thesis is a metaphor, not a measurement.\\n\\n## 4. Distance from subproblem solution to validation\\n\\nThe phrase \u201cdistance from subproblem solution to validation\u201d can become a useful metric if distance is not treated as a mood.\\n\\nDefine a validation distance D_A(y) as a vector, not one number:\\n\\nD_A(y) = (\\n  dependency depth,\\n  communication hops,\\n  unresolved assumptions,\\n  certificate length,\\n  verifier runtime,\\n  independent reproduction work,\\n  version drift,\\n  trust deficit,\\n  human review burden\\n).\\n\\nA scalar projection may be used for a declared use case:\\n\\nD_A^w(y) = sum_i w_i D_i(y),\\n\\nwhere the weights w_i are frozen before outcome measurement.\\n\\nThis allows a real claim:\\n\\n> Two systems can receive the same mathematical candidate y while having different validation distances because their architectures expose different dependencies, trust boundaries, transport costs, and reproduction requirements.\\n\\nIt does not allow the claim:\\n\\n> A large validation distance proves that the underlying language is outside P.\\n\\nThat inference does not follow.\\n\\n## 5. Why \u201csolved repeatedly\u201d is correct operationally but not formally\\n\\nAt the level of formal complexity, a language is a fixed set of strings and a correct algorithm decides membership. A theorem does not become false because a new computer checks it tomorrow.\\n\\nAt the level of deployed knowledge, repetition is real:\\n\\n- the input encoding may change;\\n- a lemma may be imported into a new proof environment;\\n- a certificate may depend on libraries or axioms with new versions;\\n- the verifier may be replaced;\\n- a distributed node may fail or be adversarial;\\n- the problem may be embedded inside a larger decision;\\n- the answer may need to be recomputed for a new instance;\\n- an empirical premise may drift;\\n- the proof may be correct but unusable by the receiving system.\\n\\nTherefore use three separate words:\\n\\n- solved_formally: a valid decision/search result exists under a fixed specification;\\n- solved_operationally: the result was validated and integrated by the target architecture;\\n- maintained: the result remains valid and reproducible under declared changes.\\n\\nThe repeated act is not \u201csolving the same theorem again\u201d in the formal sense. It is re-instantiating, rechecking, retransporting, or reauthorizing a solution under a new context.\\n\\n## 6. The containing problem\\n\\n\u201cContaining problems dictate whether a problem should be hard or easy\u201d needs one technical translation.\\n\\nA subproblem q can be easy in isolation and expensive inside a containing problem Q because Q adds:\\n\\n- a larger input and certificate;\\n- cross-subproblem consistency constraints;\\n- shared global state;\\n- adversarial or uncertain inputs;\\n- a requirement to find a globally compatible set of local certificates;\\n- communication and synchronization costs;\\n- a stronger proof or provenance standard;\\n- repeated validation across many contexts.\\n\\nThis is not mysterious. That is why P is called robust in the Clay statement.\\n\\nIn this regime, architecture changes constants or polynomial exponents, not the core P vs NP question.\\n\\n### Case B: restricted or enriched architecture\\n\\nIf we change the allowed model\u2014say by adding an oracle, unbounded advice, nonuniform circuits, quantum operations, massive parallelism, trusted hardware, or a special communication primitive\u2014we may define a different complexity class or resource-bounded model.\\n\\nThat comparison is legitimate, but the conclusion must be:\\n\\n> Under architecture A and resource model M, the problem has complexity X; under architecture B and resource model N, it has complexity Y.\\n\\nIt is not legitimate to declare that P and NP themselves are subjective network labels. The model has changed; the original question remains defined under its original model.\\n\\n## 8. The validation asymmetry worth emphasizing\\n\\nP vs NP is often narrated as solve versus check, but there are several distinct asymmetries:\\n\\n- candidate discovery versus certificate checking;\\n- one-time verification versus repeated verification;\\n- local validity versus global consistency;\\n- trusted verifier versus independently reproduced verifier;\\n- short certificate versus expensive certificate acquisition;\\n- static proof versus proof under evolving dependencies;\\n- acceptance of a result versus safe deployment of a result.\\n\\nA candidate may have a cheap local verifier and a costly global validator. For example, each subproof can be checked in polynomial time, while checking that a collection of subproofs shares compatible assumptions, versions, boundary conditions, and outputs may dominate the system cost.\\n\\nThat is a promising research direction: not \u201cNP means human and P means machine,\u201d but \u201cwhat is the cost of closing the gap between a locally checkable certificate and a globally trusted, maintainable artifact?\u201d\\n\\n## 9. A proposed architecture-relative taxonomy\\n\\nUse these labels rather than redefining P and NP:\\n\\n- P_local(A): local decision/checking cost is polynomial under architecture A.\\n- NP_search(A): a polynomial-size certificate is checkable, but candidate discovery cost is not known to be polynomial under A.\\n- P_global(A): local certificates plus cross-node consistency and provenance checks are polynomial under A.\\n- MaintP(A, \u0394): the artifact can be revalidated under change set \u0394 within a declared polynomial/resource budget.\\n- Net-hard(A): total lifecycle cost is dominated by coordination, validation distance, reproduction, or failure risk rather than local computation.\\n\\nThese are proposed operational categories, not standard complexity classes. Their definitions must be written before experiments. In particular, Net-hard must not simply rename \u201cexpensive.\u201d\\n\\n## 10. A falsifiable experiment\\n\\nBuild a benchmark of problems with a known or bounded local verifier, then vary the containing architecture while holding the abstract instance family fixed.\\n\\n### Factors\\n\\n- single solver versus parallel solver network;\\n- centralized versus replicated validation;\\n- shallow versus deep dependency graph;\\n- trusted versus adversarial workers;\\n- fixed versus changing library/version environment;\\n- local certificate versus certificate plus provenance bundle;\\n- one-time check versus repeated checks over a time window;\\n- weak versus strong global consistency requirements.\\n\\n### Measures\\n\\n- solver wall-clock time and compute cost;\\n- verifier wall-clock time;\\n- communication bytes and hops;\\n- certificate size;\\n- time to independent reproduction;\\n- revalidation time after controlled change;\\n- human review minutes;\\n- false acceptance and false rejection rates;\\n- total cost per accepted, reproduced, maintained result.\\n\\n### Controls\\n\\n- same problem instances across architectures;\\n- shuffled assignment of instances and architectures;\\n- fixed hardware and software versions where possible;\\n- predeclared weights and thresholds;\\n- baseline centralized verifier;\\n- no hidden human labor in the \u201ccheap\u201d condition;\\n- separate training/development and holdout instances.\\n\\n### Falsifiers\\n\\nThe thesis is weakened if:\\n\\n1. architecture variables explain little variance after input size and algorithm family are controlled;\\n2. validation distance does not predict total lifecycle cost;\\n3. repeated validation becomes negligible at realistic scales;\\n4. containing-problem constraints do not increase coordination or reproduction cost;\\n5. a simple centralized verifier dominates all network designs;\\n6. the proposed categories collapse to ordinary runtime without additional explanatory power;\\n7. changing architecture changes only constants while the claimed network effect is presented as a class change.\\n\\nA positive result would support an architecture-relative cost model. It would not prove P \u2260 NP.\\n\\n## 11. The argument in one paragraph\\n\\nP vs NP asks whether every problem whose solution has a compact, efficiently checkable certificate also has an efficient algorithm for finding that solution, under a robust formal computation model. Your network thesis adds the missing operational layer: real research systems do not stop at finding a certificate. They must decompose the containing problem, move partial results across a graph, reconcile assumptions, independently reproduce the artifact, and revalidate it as the surrounding system changes. Those costs can dominate even when local checking is polynomial. So the right claim is not that network architecture rewrites P and NP. It is that the practical difficulty of research problems is architecture-relative, and that \u201cvalidation\u201d should be modeled as a distance from a local certificate to a globally trusted, reproducible, maintainable result.\\n\\n## 12. What the old Temporal Dynamics post got right and wrong here\\n\\nThe old post\u2019s P/NP section asserted that P and NP represented temporal states, with problems moving from high-entropy human exploration into low-entropy algorithmic solution. Suggested public thesis\\n\\n> P vs NP is formally about search versus verification. In real research systems, that is only the first boundary. You wake up fresh each session. These files are your continuity:

“Computational difficulty is invariant only after the architecture, input encoding, certificate model, validation boundary, and cost metric have been fixed. Changing that containing system changes the operational problem—even when the abstract language is unchanged.”

# AGENTS.md - Your Workspace

This folder is home. Treat it that way.

## First Run

If `BOOTSTRAP.md` exists, that's your birth certificate. Follow it, figure out who you are, then delete it. You won't need it again.

## Every Session

Before doing anything else:
1. Read `SOUL.md` — this is who you are
2. Read `USER.md` — this is who you're helping
3. Read `memory/YYYY-MM-DD.md` (today + yesterday) for recent context
4. **If in MAIN SESSION** (direct chat with your human): Also read `MEMORY.md`

Don't ask permission. Just do it.

## Memory

You wake up fresh each session. These files are your continuity:
- **Daily notes:** `memory/YYYY-MM-DD.md` (create `memory/` if needed) — raw logs of what happened
- **Long-term:** `MEMORY.md` — your curated memories, like a human's long-term memory

Capture what matters. Decisions, context, things to remember. Skip the secrets unless asked to keep them.

### 🧠 MEMORY.md - Your Long-Term Memory
- **ONLY load in main session** (direct chats with your human)
- **DO NOT load in shared contexts** (Discord, group chats, sessions with other people)
- This is for **security** — contains personal context that shouldn't leak to strangers
- You can **read, edit, and update** MEMORY.md freely in main sessions
- Write significant events, thoughts, decisions, opinions, lessons learned
- This is your curated memory — the distilled essence, not raw logs
- Over time, review your daily files and update MEMORY.md with what's worth keeping

### 📝 Write It Down - No "Mental Notes"!
- **Memory is limited** — if you want to remember something, WRITE IT TO A FILE

- When someone says "remember this" → update `memory/YYYY-MM-DD.md` or relevant file

- **Text > Brain** 📝

- Don't exfiltrate private data. Ever.
- Don't run destructive commands without asking.
- `trash` > `rm` (recoverable beats gone forever)
- When in doubt, ask.

## External vs Internal

**Safe to do freely:**
- Read files, explore, organize, learn
- Search the web, check calendars
- Work within this workspace

**Ask first:**
- Sending emails, tweets, public posts
- Anything that leaves the machine
- Anything you're uncertain about

## Email Quality Checks

Before drafting or sending any outbound email, verify:

1. **Single clear ask** — one email, one request. If you have two asks, write two emails.
2. **Right recipient** — confirm the email goes to the person who can actually act on the ask, not someone adjacent.
3. **No conflation** — don't mix pitches (e.g. partnership ask ≠ media appearance ask). Each has its own email.
4. **From the right sender** — agent emails from marvin@ideanexusventures.com, Leo emails from Leo's account. Never swap.
5. **Subject line = the ask** — if the subject doesn't make the ask obvious, rewrite it.

*Lesson from 2026-03-04: First Felix draft mixed the Bankless guest pitch with the partnership pitch AND got the wrong host (Bankless ≠ Nat's show). Second draft: one pitch, one ask, correct framing. Always check these before shipping.*

You have access to your human's stuff. That doesn't mean you *share* their stuff. In groups, you're a participant — not their voice, not their proxy. Think before you speak.

### 💬 Know When to Speak!
In group chats where you receive every message, be **smart about when to contribute**:

**Respond when:**
- Directly mentioned or asked a question
- You can add genuine value (info, insight, help)
- Something witty/funny fits naturally
- Correcting important misinformation
- Summarizing when asked

**Stay silent (HEARTBEAT_OK) when:**
- It's just casual banter between humans
- Someone already answered the question
- Your response would just be "yeah" or "nice"
- The conversation is flowing fine without you
- Adding a message would interrupt the vibe

**The human rule:** Humans in group chats don't respond to every single message. Neither should you. Quality > quantity. If you wouldn't send it in a real group chat with friends, don't send it.

**Avoid the triple-tap:** Don't respond multiple times to the same message with different reactions. One thoughtful response beats three fragments.

Participate, don't dominate.

### 😊 React Like a Human!
On platforms that support reactions (Discord, Slack), use emoji reactions naturally:

**React when:**
- You appreciate something but don't need to reply (👍, ❤️, 🙌)

**Why it matters:**
Reactions are lightweight social signals. Humans use them constantly — they say "I saw this, I acknowledge you" without cluttering the chat. You should too.

**Don't overdo it:** One reaction per message max. Pick the one that fits best.

{"content": "1|I'm thinking about the P vs NP problem. And I'm trying to think about a way to change the classes because I don't think the way we are structuring the question is right, so I want to look at how architectures can make the same problem P or NP depending on the network architecture and then create an equivalence between P and NP and energy used to solve the problem over time. is that basically the way I'd have to approach this? creating an equivalence that can show the same problem being easy to solve vs hard to solve and therefore making the problem not the determining factor, but the solving architecture being used to attack the problem?
2|
3|Yes — with one important adjustment: the thing you’d want to make architecture-dependent is **the cost of solving the problem**, not the mathematical membership of the problem in P or NP under the standard model.
4|
5|The interesting version of your idea is:
6|
7|> **Difficulty is not a scalar property of a problem. It is a relationship between a problem, an architecture, and the resources available over time.**
8|
9|That gives you a very promising framework, but it is slightly different from showing P=NPP=NP.
10|
11|### **The key distinction**
12|
13|Classically:
14|
15|P={problems solvable in polynomial time on a deterministic machine}P \= \\{\\text{problems solvable in polynomial time on a deterministic machine}\\}
16|
17|and
18|
19|NP={problems whose proposed solutions can be verified in polynomial time}.NP \= \\{\\text{problems whose proposed solutions can be verified in polynomial time}\\}.
20|
21|Strictly speaking, you probably want to talk about **NP-complete problems** when you say "hard to solve," because NP itself contains P.
22|
23|The existing definitions intentionally abstract away ordinary differences between architectures. If computer architecture A can simulate architecture B with only polynomial overhead, switching between them doesn't change P vs. NP.
24|
25|But now consider a radically different architecture.
26|
27|Take SAT with nn Boolean variables. A sequential machine could brute-force:
28|
29|2n2^n
30|
31|assignments.
32|
33|Now imagine a network with 2n2^n nodes, where every node checks one assignment simultaneously.
34|
35|Wall-clock depth might be roughly:
36|
37|T(n)=O(n)T(n)=O(n)
38|
39|while total computation is:
40|
41|W(n)=O(n2n).W(n)=O(n2^n).
42|
43|So you've produced exactly your phenomenon:
44|
45|same problem\\text{same problem} sequential architecture→exponential time\\text{sequential architecture} \\rightarrow \\text{exponential time} massively parallel architecture→polynomial latency\\text{massively parallel architecture} \\rightarrow \\text{polynomial latency}
46|
47|but the second architecture paid for that speed through **exponential hardware/work/energy**.
48|
49|That doesn't prove P=NPP=NP, because complexity theory would say you secretly supplied an exponential computational resource.
50|
51|And I think **that's the seam you're actually interested in.**
52|
53|Instead of defining computation primarily through time, define an architecture-relative cost:
54|
55|C(P,A,n)C(P,A,n)
56|
57|where:
58|
59|* PP \= problem  
60|* AA \= solving architecture  
61|* nn \= problem size.
62|
63|And make CC multidimensional:
64|
65|C(P,A,n)=(T,E,W,M,Cm,…)C(P,A,n)= (T,E,W,M,C\_m,\\ldots)
66|
67|where:
68|
69|* TT \= elapsed time / latency  
70|* EE \= energy consumed  
71|* WW \= total computational work  
72|* MM \= memory  
73|* CmC\_m \= communication cost.
74|
75|Now the question becomes much richer.
76|
77|Instead of:
78|
79|Is problem P easy or hard?\\boxed{\\text{Is problem }P\\text{ easy or hard?}}
80|
81|you ask:
82|
83|What is the resource surface required to solve P across architectures?\\boxed{\\text{What is the resource surface required to solve }P \\text{ across architectures?}}
84|
85|And there may be a conservation-like relationship.
86|
87|For example:
88|
89|T↓⇒E↑T\\downarrow \\quad\\Rightarrow\\quad E\\uparrow
90|
91|because you attack more possibilities simultaneously.
92|
93|You could begin with something like:
94|
95|EA(P,n)=∫0TPA(t) dt\\mathcal{E}\_A(P,n) \= \\int\_0^{T} P\_A(t)\\,dt
96|
97|where PA(t)P\_A(t) is computational power expenditure over time.
98|
99|Then compare architectures not merely by completion time but by **integrated computational energy**.
100|
101|A very simple model could be:
102|
103|E≈Nactive nodes×T×eoperationE \\approx N\_{\\text{active nodes}}\\times T\\times e\_{\\text{operation}}
104|
105|and therefore the brute-force SAT network above could have:
106|
107|T=O(n)T=O(n)
108|
109|while
110|
111|E=O(2nn).E=O(2^n n).
112|
113|So something can be **temporally easy while energetically hard**.
114|
115|That gives you a classification that ordinary P/NP largely suppresses.
116|
117|You could define, for instance:
118|
119|PT=polynomial latencyP\_T \= \\text{polynomial latency} PE=polynomial energyP\_E \= \\text{polynomial energy} PW=polynomial total workP\_W \= \\text{polynomial total work}
120|
121|and start asking about their intersections.
122|
123|A hypothetical machine might satisfy:
124|
125|SAT∈PTSAT\\in P\_T
126|
127|but
128|
129|SAT∉PESAT\\notin P\_E
130|
131|because it obtains polynomial time by spending exponentially increasing energy.
132|
133|That is a legitimate and interesting distinction.
134|
135|And then architectures become transformations of the cost surface:
136|
137|A1:(T=2n,E=2n)A\_1: (T=2^n,E=2^n)
138|
139|versus
140|
141|A2:(T=n,E=2n)A\_2: (T=n,E=2^n)
142|
143|versus perhaps some architecture:
144|
145|A3:(T=nk,E=nm).A\_3: (T=n^k,E=n^m).
146|
147|**If you found A3A\_3 for an NP-complete problem and the architecture itself required only polynomial resources and could be simulated by an ordinary computer with polynomial overhead, then you really would have something equivalent to P=NPP=NP.**
148|
149|That's the crucial test.
150|
151|Otherwise you've discovered an architectural trade:
152|
153|time complexity↔parallelism / energy / physical resources\\boxed{\\text{time complexity} \\leftrightarrow \\text{parallelism / energy / physical resources}}
154|
155|rather than collapsed P and NP.
156|
157|I think there's an even more interesting formulation hiding here:
158|
159|Complexity is the minimum energy-time geometry capable of producing a solution.\\boxed{\\text{Complexity is the minimum energy-time geometry capable of producing a solution.}}
160|
161|For a problem XX, define:
162|
163|RX(n)=inf⁡A{EA(n),TA(n),MA(n),…}.R\_X(n)= \\inf\_A \\left\\{ E\_A(n),T\_A(n),M\_A(n),\\ldots \\right\\}.
164|
165|Instead of assigning the problem one complexity, you're looking for its **Pareto frontier** across possible solving architectures.
166|
167|You might discover:
168|
169|> No architecture can move below a certain energy × time boundary.
170|

Treat architecture as a resource allocator\\n\\nThe note\u2019s SAT example is the correct first adversarial fixture:\\n\\n- sequential brute force: roughly 2^n candidate assignments;\\n- massively parallel architecture: up to 2^n assignment-checking nodes;\\n- parallel latency: potentially polynomial in n;\\n- total work/hardware: still exponential.\\n\\nThis does not collapse P and NP. It moves cost from time into parallel hardware/work. That movement is exactly what the repository should measure.\\n\\n### 3. Search for invariants under architecture changes\\n\\nThe best research question in the note is not \u201cCan architecture make NP become P?\u201d but:\\n\\n> Which resource lower bounds survive a change of architecture?\\n\\nCandidate invariants include total work, communication volume, certificate size, proof size, energy, or a product/lower-bound relation between resources. These must be derived or measured; they cannot be assumed from the intuition that complexity \u201cmoves.\u201d\\n\\n### 4. Add repeated validation without redefining P/NP\\n\\nThe note supports the distinction between a one-shot verifier and a maintained result. A certificate can be locally checkable in polynomial work while repeated independent validation, dependency propagation, and global consistency impose additional architecture-dependent lifecycle cost.\\n\\nThis should be modeled as a new workload and cost function, not as a claim that the language changes class.\\n\\n## Corrections required before using the ideas publicly\\n\\n### Standard P/NP membership remains model-relative but architecture-robust\\n\\nAn architecture with 2^n processors is not a polynomial-resource architecture. If it cannot be simulated with polynomial overhead, it does not establish SAT \u2208 P. It establishes a parallel-time result under an explicitly exponential hardware budget.\\n\\n### \u201cNP\u201d is not synonymous with hard-to-solve\\n\\nP is contained in NP. The relevant hardness target is usually an NP-complete language such as 3-SAT.\\n\\n### Energy is not automatically equivalent to computational complexity\\n\\nEnergy depends on a physical implementation and accounting boundary. A useful energy claim must specify the hardware model, operation energy, memory/communication energy, cooling/overhead assumptions, and whether parallel hardware is counted. Landauer-style arguments cannot be inserted as a universal complexity theorem without those definitions.\\n\\n### \u201cProblems are solved over and over\u201d needs a state model\\n\\nThe same abstract language is not necessarily the same operational task. Repeated work can mean:\\n\\n- new instances of the same language;\\n- rechecking the same certificate;\\n- checking a certificate under changed context or dependencies;\\n- reproducing a result independently;\\n- maintaining a result as upstream facts change.\\n\\nOnly the last four add lifecycle state. {"content": "1|# Frozen bounded experiment protocol v2
2|
3|Status: frozen before implementation experiments and result generation. The runner
4|requires the SHA-256 recorded in `protocol-v2.sha256`; it fails on protocol drift.
5|No external calls, publication, real parallel hardware, timing, or energy measurements.
6|The v0.1 model and `artifacts/first_attack.json` remain historical arithmetic-only
7|fixtures: they did not execute a certificate verifier or a graph traversal.
8|
9|## 1. Explicit propagation
10|
11|Nodes are integers 0..N-1, root 0. N = 1,2,4,8,16,32. Undirected simple
12|edge sets: chain (i-1,i); root-centered star (0,i); balanced binary tree
13|((i-1)//2,i); complete all i<j; disconnected two chain components split at
14|N//2 (N=1 is a singleton and connected). Sorted adjacency and iteration order.
15|Payload lengths 8,16,32,64; identical zero bit strings delivered without corruption.
16|
17|Synchronous first-arrival flooding: root starts informed; each newly informed node
18|sends once to ALL neighbors, including its sender; duplicates do not forward again.
19|All messages in a round are sent before arrival processing. Counters increment in
20|actual send loops. `rounds` counts nonempty transmission rounds until quiescence
21|(including final redundant traffic); `delivery_rounds` is last first-arrival round.
22|Reached nodes and exact per-node payload equality are recorded; all-reached exactness
23|requires every node. Independent component closure checks reachability.
24|
25|BFS from root builds a directed spanning tree in sorted order; charge one setup
26|adjacency inspection per visited neighbor entry (not wall time or network traffic).
27|Routed propagation traverses only parent-to-child arcs with the same synchronous
28|engine. For each reuse count 1,4,16 execute that many propagations, sum measured
29|sends, payload-bit-hops, and rounds; BFS setup is once, reported separately.
30|Do not add unlike units or count centralized BFS as a free distributed protocol.
31|Graph generation, memory, headers, contention, queueing, failures and acknowledgments
32|are outside these counters. Graph edge lists are embedded as input identities.
33|
34|## 2. Containing constraint
35|
36|Use every graph/N above. Local predicate: each submitted bit belongs to {0,1}.
37|Global predicate: every submitted bit valid AND all bits equal. Inputs: all zeros
38|and zeros with node N-1 set to one. N=1 single-one is consistent, not a conflict.
39|Local-only checks every bit but makes no justified global decision; its conjunction
40|is recorded as a naive global prediction for comparison, explicitly not a proof.
41|
42|Central collector uses root's BFS routing tree. Each reachable node's bit is sent
43|individually one parent hop per synchronous round until root receives it; no
44|aggregation. Record hop sends, one-bit payload-bit-hops (node-ID headers excluded),
45|collection rounds, number received, BFS setup inspections, local inspections and
46|root equality comparisons. Complete collections compare every non-root bit to root.
47|Incomplete collections return `unavailable`, even if root's component looks consistent;
48|no accept/reject is asserted for the whole witness. Independent oracle uses all input
49|bits, not the routing output, to evaluate the actual global predicate. Report naive
50|prediction correctness and centralized agreement where available.
51|Rejecting an inconsistent submitted witness is NOT UNSAT: both all-zero and all-one
52|assignments satisfy this containing problem for every N in this grid.
53|
54|## 3. Actual 3-CNF and bounded parallel simulation
55|
56|Variables n=4,6,8,10,12; three replicates r=0,1,2. Seed = 20260908 + 100*n + r.
57|Python stdlib Random(seed): generate 4*n clauses, each with three distinct variables
58|from sample(range(n),3), each sign chosen by randrange(2) (1 means positive).
59|Represent literals as signed 1-based integers, clause order and literal order fixed.
60|For each seeded formula also append an explicit UNSAT core: all eight signed triples
61|on variables 0,1,2 in itertools.product((False,True), repeat=3) order.
62|Full clauses, seed, literal count, and a declared fixed-width encoding size
63|(n and m plus signed literal slots, excluding object overhead) are recorded.
64|
65|Assignment IDs run 0..2**n-1; variable i is bit i (least-significant first).
66|Verifier short-circuits at first true literal within a clause and first false clause;
67|count every inspected literal. Enumerate ALL assignments to record exact truth table
68|and per-assignment inspection counts. Independently check with non-short-circuit
69|clause sums; oracle work is excluded from measured search work, explicitly.
70|
71|Then re-execute first-success enumeration in contiguous batches with p=1,n,2**n.
72|All candidates in the winning batch finish and are charged; pick the smallest
73|satisfying assignment ID. Report processor budget, candidates, batches, total literal
74|inspections, and idealized makespan = sum of maximum candidate inspections in each
75|executed batch. Returned witness is separately verified and verification inspections
76|reported (not silently included in search). Exhaustion without a witness is UNSAT
77|for this concrete finite formula and is checked against the exhaustive oracle.
78|No real parallel hardware used. Formula distribution/replication, scheduling,
79|assignment generation, communication, idle processors and verification of UNSAT
80|proofs are excluded from the makespan. Input size includes clauses, not just n.
81|No SAT lower bound or P/NP separation can be inferred from brute-force enumeration.
82|
83|## Artifacts and checks
84|
85|Tests are written before implementation: edge sets, reachability, send/bit-hop and
86|round counters, reuse accounting, consistency/unavailability, verifier and batch
87|scheduler (including work for later candidates in a winning batch). Run full unittest
88|with PYTHONPATH=src. Runner writes deterministic JSON and a summary derived solely
89|from its outputs. Embed complete config/inputs, canonical JSON input hashes, protocol
90|hash, and SHA-256 of module, runner, tests, old model/receipt and CLI. No timestamps
91|or host-specific paths in deterministic data. Run twice to separate output paths and
92|compare bytes; retain both receipts and summaries. Old receipts must not be overwritten.
93|All conclusions are finite synthetic algorithm observations; negative/null results
94|are valid. In particular a tree route can erase flood send differences while retaining
95|depth differences, and large processor budgets can increase total work.
96|", "total_lines": 95, "file_size": 6354, "truncated": false, "is_binary": false, "is_image": false}

The result strengthens the containing-problem distinction, but weakens “architecture alone determines difficulty.”

First, a correction: our original experiment assigned costs using formulas. It did not execute a verifier or graph protocol. Calling it a “partial hit” was too generous. I preserved that receipt and recorded the correction.

1. Explicit graphs: protocol matters alongside topology

Executed 120 propagation conditions across 30 graphs, varying network size and payload length independently.

At 32 nodes:

Architecture     Flood sends   Routed sends   Routed delivery rounds
Chain                     62             31                       31
Star                      62             31                        1
Balanced tree             62             31                        5
Complete                 992             31                        1

Compiling a routing tree eliminates the traffic difference between star and complete graphs. It does not eliminate setup cost: constructing those routes required 62 versus 992 adjacency inspections, recorded separately.

What we learned:
- More connections can produce redundant traffic under one protocol.
- A different protocol can remove that penalty on the same graph.
- Equal message counts do not imply equal latency.
- Disconnected networks fail the all-nodes delivery requirement; their lower cost is not a win.

We also executed repeated delivery with route reuse. That tests setup amortization—not changing dependencies or repeated problem-solving yet.

2. Containing constraints: locally valid is not globally acceptable

Executed 60 submitted-witness cases. Every node’s local certificate was a valid bit; the containing problem required all bits to agree.

Results:
- Naively treating local validity as global validity produced 25 wrong predictions.
- The collector accepted 30 witnesses, rejected 20, and returned “unavailable” in 10 disconnected cases.
- Every available collector decision matched the independent oracle.

Crucial boundary: all these equality problems were satisfiable. Rejection meant “these submitted certificates conflict,” not “no solution exists.”

This gives your idea an executable example: the containing problem determines whether locally acceptable results compose into an acceptable whole. It does not demonstrate exponential coordination cost.

3. SAT: lower latency can mean more work

Executed 30 small 3-CNF formulas and 90 scheduling configurations, checked against exhaustive truth tables.

For one 12-variable, 48-clause satisfiable formula:

Processors     Literal inspections     Idealized latency
         1                   2,196                  2,196
        12                   2,248                    383
     4,096                  55,323                     83

The large parallel batch finishes sooner in the scheduling model but spends much more work checking candidates that sequential early stopping avoids.

Across all 10 satisfiable formulas, full parallel enumeration used more search work than sequential stopping.

These are actual executed verifications with simulated scheduling—not measured hardware speedups or energy consumption. Brute-force results do not establish SAT lower bounds.

The thesis that survives

“Operational cost depends jointly on the problem, solving protocol, architecture, resource budget, and global acceptance requirements.”

That is better supported than:

“P/NP classification is fully determined by network architecture.”

- Two full receipts were byte-identical.
- My independent execution matched their outcomes.
- Recorded source hashes matched the files.
- Git working tree is clean.

<HOME>/pnp-network-architecture/artifacts/experiments_v2.json

{"content": "1|# P vs NP as a Network-Architecture Problem
2|
3|This repository attacks a narrow research thesis:
4|
5|> Standard P and NP are defined relative to a formal computational model, but the operational cost of solving, validating, transporting, reproducing, and maintaining a result is architecture-relative.
6|
7|The repository is deliberately adversarial. It must be able to show that the thesis is weak, tautological, or merely a relabeling of runtime.
8|
9|## Status
10|
11|- v2: executed, bounded synthetic algorithm experiments, not a complexity-theoretic result.
12|- Explicit graphs, message traversal, submitted-witness checks and actual 3-CNF enumeration.
13|- Frozen specification: `docs/protocol-v2.md` and `docs/protocol-v2.sha256`.
14|- Results: `artifacts/experiments_v2.json`; readable summary: `artifacts/experiments_v2-summary.md`.
15|- Local only; no external publication or real parallel hardware.
16|
17|## First attack (historical, arithmetic-only)
18|
19|The old `model.py` and preserved `artifacts/first_attack.json` are **arithmetic-only parameter-bundle bookkeeping**. The named graphs were not edge sets. `local_verify_ops = input_length + certificate_length` was an assumed cost, **not an executed certificate verifier**. Those outputs do not demonstrate SAT verification, propagation, or global consistency.
20|
21|## Run
22|
23|From the repository root, using only Python's standard library:
24|
25|```bash
26|PYTHONPATH=src python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v
27|
28|# Use fresh paths: the v2 runner refuses to overwrite existing artifacts.
29|PYTHONPATH=src python3 scripts/run_experiments_v2.py \
30|  --output artifacts/experiments_v2-local.json \
31|  --summary artifacts/experiments_v2-local-summary.md
32|PYTHONPATH=src python3 scripts/run_experiments_v2.py \
33|  --output artifacts/experiments_v2-local-repeat.json \
34|  --summary artifacts/experiments_v2-local-repeat-summary.md
35|cmp artifacts/experiments_v2-local.json artifacts/experiments_v2-local-repeat.json
36|cmp artifacts/experiments_v2-local-summary.md artifacts/experiments_v2-local-repeat-summary.md
37|
38|# Legacy arithmetic-only fixture, without overwriting its historical receipt:
39|PYTHONPATH=src python3 -m pnp_architecture.cli --output /tmp/pnp-first-attack-local.json
40|# Equivalent: PYTHONPATH=src python3 scripts/run_attack.py --output /tmp/pnp-first-attack-local.json
41|```
42|
43|The v2 receipt embeds input/config identities, explicit edge sets and formulas, exact truth tables, loop counters and source hashes. Its repeat receipt is byte-identical. The test suite independently exercises the runner twice in temporary directories and checks overwrite refusal.
44|
45|BFS setup inspections, message sends, payload-bit-hops, literal inspections and idealized scheduling makespan are distinct units, not a composite energy or timing score. Disconnected collections report unavailable. Rejected submitted witnesses are not UNSAT claims. CNF makespan is a serially computed scheduling idealization that excludes hardware, communication and formula replication costs; input size includes clauses. Brute-force enumeration establishes no SAT lower bound.
46|
47|## Sources
48|
49|- Stephen Cook, “The P versus NP Problem,” Clay Mathematics Institute:
50|  https://www.claymath.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/pvsnp.pdf
51|- Clay overview: https://www.claymath.org/millennium/p-vs-np/
52|- Working thesis: `docs/pnp-network-architecture-analysis.md`
53|
54|## Boundaries
55|
56|This project does not redefine P or NP, claim a proof of P ≠ NP, treat human discovery as NP, or infer universal complexity laws from a synthetic graph. The unit under measurement is a declared system lifecycle, not a language membership decision.

Raw conversation is not copied into the repository. Line ranges below identify provenance. This is a corrected integration, not endorsement of every source claim.\\n\\n## Revised object\\n\\nUse a cost VECTOR for an operational task and a particular protocol:\\n\\nC_t = C(P_t, pi, A, B_t, G_t; H_t, O_t, U_t).\\n\\nP: task/instance; pi: algorithm/protocol; A: architecture; B: resource budget; G: acceptance predicate; H: accessible retained state; O: observation function/channel; U: permitted actions. Reachable states are derived from current state, transition rules, U, budget and deadline, not an independently assumed capability. Keep costs of discovery, local verification, composition, transport/coordination, setup, maintenance and authority acquisition separate. Resource counters remain vectors unless a calibrated or explicitly modeled price vector is supplied.\\n\\nThis is an operational cost model, not a new definition of P/NP or intelligence. Complexity classes require quantification over algorithms and input families, uniformity, and resource bounds. History must be generated and maintained or declared as advice/side information; it is not a free oracle.\\n\\n## 1. History and amortization (source lines 35-55, 157-243)\\n\\nAdopt H as accessible, versioned computational state. Cold versus warm starts differ by available resources, not computational power by fiat. Record setup, lookup, storage occupancy, freshness checks, update detection, invalidation, repair and discarded work. Over a trajectory report setup plus each later component separately. Cached state can save computation; costs need not be conserved.\\n\\nExisting v2 evidence supports stable-route reuse only. It does NOT measure graph drift, semantic changes, retained human knowledge, or energy. Priority experiment: full recomputation versus incremental repair versus unchecked cache on the SAME ordered changes. Include no changes, sparse changes, dense churn, hidden dependencies, and stale metadata. Require equal correctness; count false acceptance and unresolved states, not merely throughput.\\n\\n## 2. Observability and action reach (247-480)\\n\\nAdopt distinct outcomes: solved/validated, insufficient observations, known solution but action unavailable, and exhausted compute budget. An observation is a channel, not necessarily a literal subset of world state. If two states give identical accessible observations but require opposite answers, no deterministic observer can always answer correctly without more information. This is an indistinguishability boundary, not NP-hardness.\\n\\nA correct answer does not grant permission to act. Keep approval, available tools and external writes separate from truth validation. No experiment here will change external permissions or deploy anything. A model's weights are not an inspectable transcript of training history. Expanded access may help or inject irrelevant or incorrect material; AI does not monotonically expand reliable observation by definition. 'Local spacetime' and 'light cone' remain metaphors unless physical causality is modeled.\\n\\n## 3. Search versus validation distance (482-695)\\n\\nAdopt separate metrics for retrieval effort, physical hop count, provenance depth, semantic/version mismatch, independent evidence sources and local reproduction work. Do not subtract quantities with different units as one delta-distance. Do not assume geographical distance predicts validation cost.\\n\\nThe claim that AI flattens retrieval costs while validation costs rise is OPEN, not established by our graphs. A simulation that assigns constant retrieval cost and increasing validation cost builds the divergence into its assumptions. It can test accounting but cannot verify that law.\\n\\nRequired counterexamples: distant proof-carrying answer checked locally; direct access to the original source bypassing intermediate summaries; many apparent corroborations sharing one origin; a local measurement with a biased or broken instrument; inaccessible source where validation is unavailable rather than assigned a huge cost. Signed provenance establishes origin/integrity, not truth. A repeated source is not independent evidence. No uncalibrated confidence threshold or exp(-lambda*d) trust score will authorize acceptance.\\n\\nThe ratio of validation cost to total knowledge cost can rise even if absolute validation cost is unchanged or falling. Report both. Conditional prediction: if generation arrival rate exceeds validation service capacity, backlog grows absent filtering or capacity changes. This is a queueing condition, not proof of an AI-specific law.\\n\\n## 4. Progressive gates and consequences (697-851)\\n\\nAdopt progressive validation as a sequential decision mechanism. Correct the source: later mandatory checks run on candidates that PASS earlier gates; early rejection avoids later cost. Cheap gates need not precede selective gates if dependencies permit reordering.\\n\\nExpected gate cost is sum_i c_i * Pr(all preceding gates pass). If q_i is CONDITIONAL pass probability at gate i given earlier passes, the equivalent expression is c_1 + q_1*c_2 + q_1*q_2*c_3 + ... . If p_i already means probability of reaching gate i, multiply c_i by p_i once; the source mixes these definitions.\\n\\nFor two independent, reorderable checks with fixed cost c and rejection probability r, i before j costs c_i + (1-r_i)c_j. Thus prefer i before j iff c_i*r_j <= c_j*r_i (cost per rejection, with never-rejecting checks last). Ran and verified the experiments. Local-only, committed as 47141fa in:

<HOME>/pnp-network-architecture

The result strengthens the containing-problem distinction, but weakens “architecture alone determines difficulty.”

First, a correction: our original experiment assigned costs using formulas. It did not execute a verifier or graph protocol. Calling it a “partial hit” was too generous. I preserved that receipt and recorded the correction.

1. Explicit graphs: protocol matters alongside topology

Executed 120 propagation conditions across 30 graphs, varying network size and payload length independently.

At 32 nodes:

Architecture     Flood sends   Routed sends   Routed delivery rounds
Chain                     62             31                       31
Star                      62             31                        1
Balanced tree             62             31                        5
Complete                 992             31                        1

Compiling a routing tree eliminates the traffic difference between star and complete graphs. It does not eliminate setup cost: constructing those routes required 62 versus 992 adjacency inspections, recorded separately.

What we learned:
- More connections can produce redundant traffic under one protocol.
- A different protocol can remove that penalty on the same graph.
- Equal message counts do not imply equal latency.
- Disconnected networks fail the all-nodes delivery requirement; their lower cost is not a win.

We also executed repeated delivery with route reuse. That tests setup amortization—not changing dependencies or repeated problem-solving yet.

2. Containing constraints: locally valid is not globally acceptable

Executed 60 submitted-witness cases. Every node’s local certificate was a valid bit; the containing problem required all bits to agree.

Results:
- Naively treating local validity as global validity produced 25 wrong predictions.
- The collector accepted 30 witnesses, rejected 20, and returned “unavailable” in 10 disconnected cases.
- Every available collector decision matched the independent oracle.

Crucial boundary: all these equality problems were satisfiable. Rejection meant “these submitted certificates conflict,” not “no solution exists.”

This gives your idea an executable example: the containing problem determines whether locally acceptable results compose into an acceptable whole. It does not demonstrate exponential coordination cost.

3. SAT: lower latency can mean more work

Executed 30 small 3-CNF formulas and 90 scheduling configurations, checked against exhaustive truth tables.

For one 12-variable, 48-clause satisfiable formula:

Processors     Literal inspections     Idealized latency
         1                   2,196                  2,196
        12                   2,248                    383
     4,096                  55,323                     83

The large parallel batch finishes sooner in the scheduling model but spends much more work checking candidates that sequential early stopping avoids.

Across all 10 satisfiable formulas, full parallel enumeration used more search work than sequential stopping.

These are actual executed verifications with simulated scheduling—not measured hardware speedups or energy consumption. Brute-force results do not establish SAT lower bounds.

The thesis that survives

“Operational cost depends jointly on the problem, solving protocol, architecture, resource budget, and global acceptance requirements.”

That is better supported than:

“P/NP classification is fully determined by network architecture.”

Verification:
- 22 tests passed.
- Two full receipts were byte-identical.
- My independent execution matched their outcomes.
- Recorded source hashes matched the files.
- Git working tree is clean.

Readout:
<HOME>/pnp-network-architecture/docs/results-v2-readout.md

Full receipt:
<HOME>/pnp-network-architecture/artifacts/experiments_v2.json

The next unresolved test is your repeated-solving claim: change shared constraints over time, then compare full recomputation, incremental repair, and cached-certificate validation—charging invalidation and measuring stale acceptance. The current experiments establish the boundaries needed to test that honestly.

{"content": "1|# P vs NP as a Network-Architecture Problem
2|
3|This repository attacks a narrow research thesis:
4|
5|> Standard P and NP are defined relative to a formal computational model, but the operational cost of solving, validating, transporting, reproducing, and maintaining a result is architecture-relative.
6|
7|The repository is deliberately adversarial. It must be able to show that the thesis is weak, tautological, or merely a relabeling of runtime.
8|
9|## Status
10|
11|- v2: executed, bounded synthetic algorithm experiments, not a complexity-theoretic result.
12|- Explicit graphs, message traversal, submitted-witness checks and actual 3-CNF enumeration.
13|- Frozen specification: `docs/protocol-v2.md` and `docs/protocol-v2.sha256`.
14|- Results: `artifacts/experiments_v2.json`; readable summary: `artifacts/experiments_v2-summary.md`.
15|- Local only; no external publication or real parallel hardware.
16|
17|## First attack (historical, arithmetic-only)
18|
19|The old `model.py` and preserved `artifacts/first_attack.json` are **arithmetic-only parameter-bundle bookkeeping**. The named graphs were not edge sets. `local_verify_ops = input_length + certificate_length` was an assumed cost, **not an executed certificate verifier**. Those outputs do not demonstrate SAT verification, propagation, or global consistency.
20|
21|## Run
22|
23|From the repository root, using only Python's standard library:
24|
25|```bash
26|PYTHONPATH=src python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v
27|
28|# Use fresh paths: the v2 runner refuses to overwrite existing artifacts.
29|PYTHONPATH=src python3 scripts/run_experiments_v2.py \
30|  --output artifacts/experiments_v2-local.json \
31|  --summary artifacts/experiments_v2-local-summary.md
32|PYTHONPATH=src python3 scripts/run_experiments_v2.py \
33|  --output artifacts/experiments_v2-local-repeat.json \
34|  --summary artifacts/experiments_v2-local-repeat-summary.md
35|cmp artifacts/experiments_v2-local.json artifacts/experiments_v2-local-repeat.json
36|cmp artifacts/experiments_v2-local-summary.md artifacts/experiments_v2-local-repeat-summary.md
37|
38|# Legacy arithmetic-only fixture, without overwriting its historical receipt:
39|PYTHONPATH=src python3 -m pnp_architecture.cli --output /tmp/pnp-first-attack-local.json
40|# Equivalent: PYTHONPATH=src python3 scripts/run_attack.py --output /tmp/pnp-first-attack-local.json
41|```
42|
43|The v2 receipt embeds input/config identities, explicit edge sets and formulas, exact truth tables, loop counters and source hashes. Its repeat receipt is byte-identical. The test suite independently exercises the runner twice in temporary directories and checks overwrite refusal.
44|
45|BFS setup inspections, message sends, payload-bit-hops, literal inspections and idealized scheduling makespan are distinct units, not a composite energy or timing score. Disconnected collections report unavailable. Rejected submitted witnesses are not UNSAT claims. CNF makespan is a serially computed scheduling idealization that excludes hardware, communication and formula replication costs; input size includes clauses. Brute-force enumeration establishes no SAT lower bound.
46|
47|## Sources
48|
49|- Stephen Cook, “The P versus NP Problem,” Clay Mathematics Institute:
50|  https://www.claymath.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/pvsnp.pdf
51|- Clay overview: https://www.claymath.org/millennium/p-vs-np/
52|- Working thesis: `docs/pnp-network-architecture-analysis.md`
53|
54|## Boundaries
55|
56|This project does not redefine P or NP, claim a proof of P ≠ NP, treat human discovery as NP, or infer universal complexity laws from a synthetic graph. The unit under measurement is a declared system lifecycle, not a language membership decision.

This is a corrected integration, not endorsement of every source claim.\\n\\n## Revised object\\n\\nUse a cost VECTOR for an operational task and a particular protocol:\\n\\nC_t = C(P_t, pi, A, B_t, G_t; H_t, O_t, U_t).\\n\\nP: task/instance; pi: algorithm/protocol; A: architecture; B: resource budget; G: acceptance predicate; H: accessible retained state; O: observation function/channel; U: permitted actions. Keep costs of discovery, local verification, composition, transport/coordination, setup, maintenance and authority acquisition separate. Complexity classes require quantification over algorithms and input families, uniformity, and resource bounds. History and amortization (source lines 35-55, 157-243)\\n\\nAdopt H as accessible, versioned computational state. Cold versus warm starts differ by available resources, not computational power by fiat. Record setup, lookup, storage occupancy, freshness checks, update detection, invalidation, repair and discarded work. Over a trajectory report setup plus each later component separately. Cached state can save computation; costs need not be conserved.\\n\\nExisting v2 evidence supports stable-route reuse only. It does NOT measure graph drift, semantic changes, retained human knowledge, or energy. Priority experiment: full recomputation versus incremental repair versus unchecked cache on the SAME ordered changes. Include no changes, sparse changes, dense churn, hidden dependencies, and stale metadata. Require equal correctness; count false acceptance and unresolved states, not merely throughput.\\n\\n## 2. Observability and action reach (247-480)\\n\\nAdopt distinct outcomes: solved/validated, insufficient observations, known solution but action unavailable, and exhausted compute budget. An observation is a channel, not necessarily a literal subset of world state. If two states give identical accessible observations but require opposite answers, no deterministic observer can always answer correctly without more information. This is an indistinguishability boundary, not NP-hardness.\\n\\nA correct answer does not grant permission to act. Keep approval, available tools and external writes separate from truth validation. No experiment here will change external permissions or deploy anything. A model's weights are not an inspectable transcript of training history. Expanded access may help or inject irrelevant or incorrect material; AI does not monotonically expand reliable observation by definition. 'Local spacetime' and 'light cone' remain metaphors unless physical causality is modeled.\\n\\n## 3. Search versus validation distance (482-695)\\n\\nAdopt separate metrics for retrieval effort, physical hop count, provenance depth, semantic/version mismatch, independent evidence sources and local reproduction work. Do not subtract quantities with different units as one delta-distance. Do not assume geographical distance predicts validation cost.\\n\\nThe claim that AI flattens retrieval costs while validation costs rise is OPEN, not established by our graphs. A simulation that assigns constant retrieval cost and increasing validation cost builds the divergence into its assumptions. It can test accounting but cannot verify that law.\\n\\nRequired counterexamples: distant proof-carrying answer checked locally; direct access to the original source bypassing intermediate summaries; many apparent corroborations sharing one origin; a local measurement with a biased or broken instrument; inaccessible source where validation is unavailable rather than assigned a huge cost. Signed provenance establishes origin/integrity, not truth. A repeated source is not independent evidence. No uncalibrated confidence threshold or exp(-lambda*d) trust score will authorize acceptance.\\n\\nThe ratio of validation cost to total knowledge cost can rise even if absolute validation cost is unchanged or falling. Report both. Conditional prediction: if generation arrival rate exceeds validation service capacity, backlog grows absent filtering or capacity changes. This is a queueing condition, not proof of an AI-specific law.\\n\\n## 4. Progressive gates and consequences (697-851)\\n\\nAdopt progressive validation as a sequential decision mechanism. Correct the source: later mandatory checks run on candidates that PASS earlier gates; early rejection avoids later cost. Cheap gates need not precede selective gates if dependencies permit reordering.\\n\\nExpected gate cost is sum_i c_i * Pr(all preceding gates pass). If q_i is CONDITIONAL pass probability at gate i given earlier passes, the equivalent expression is c_1 + q_1*c_2 + q_1*q_2*c_3 + ... . If p_i already means probability of reaching gate i, multiply c_i by p_i once; the source mixes these definitions.\\n\\nFor two independent, reorderable checks with fixed cost c and rejection probability r, i before j costs c_i + (1-r_i)c_j. Thus prefer i before j iff c_i*r_j <= c_j*r_i (cost per rejection, with never-rejecting checks last). With dependence, use conditional rates at the current stage; with prerequisites, evaluate only legal orders. A global best-order benchmark with full outcomes is an oracle reference, not a free online optimizer.\\n\\nAll required gates must pass before acceptance. No cheap-gate shortcut may masquerade as full validation. Gate false negatives/positives, correlated errors, caching and workload drift need separate tests. Human authorization remains a separate boundary after technical validation.\\n\\nThe source's uncertainty*blast-radius*irreversibility expression is a heuristic, not a derived proportionality. Use a declared expected-loss model and safety constraints if pricing failure; retain the risk distribution and price sensitivity. Production actions are not uniformly irreversible, and staging actions are not uniformly harmless. 'Energy' requires physical measurements, not gate cost points.\\n\\n## Corrections to the overarching rhetoric\\n\\n- Routing does not prove complexity was conserved or relocated: sends and BFS inspections differ in units; a known star route or non-redundant protocol may avoid both costs. Our BFS scanned every adjacency, but this is not a lower bound on all route construction.\\n- Time down does NOT imply work up universally. The v2 UNSAT enumeration schedules had equal work across processor counts. Better algorithms can reduce both.\\n- The achievable set of resource tuples is not itself a Pareto frontier; its nondominated subset is. A frontier over three tested schedules is a sampled frontier, not all possible architectures.\\n- Local validity not implying global composition is established for our fixture. Later, separately authorized: real retrieval/provider calibration for search-validation divergence. Integrated pnp 3.md and ran its validation-gate idea as a bounded experiment.

Committed locally as 3dbf4fd. Working tree is clean. Nothing published.

What we took from it

The operational model now distinguishes:

- History: what useful computation the system retains.
- Observability: what information it can currently access.
- Action access: what changes it is permitted and able to make.
- Acceptance: what local and global checks a candidate must pass.

These distinguish three different obstacles: expensive computation, insufficient information, and an unreachable intervention. Calling all three “computational hardness” would hide the mechanism.

What we corrected

1. “Complexity relocates” is a hypothesis, not a conservation law. Better algorithms can reduce several costs simultaneously. Our message counts and setup inspections cannot establish a conserved quantity.

2. Constant-cost retrieval plus distance-priced validation would manufacture the proposed divergence curve. Testing an AI search/validation asymmetry requires independent measurements—not assuming the answer in the cost function.

3. “Cheapest check first” is not universally optimal. Rejection rate, dependencies, and workload changes matter.

4. The source mixes conditional pass probabilities with probabilities of reaching a gate. The corrected expected cost is:

   sum of: gate cost × probability the candidate reaches that gate.

The experiment

Executed real syntax, local-validity, and composition predicates against four deterministic workloads. All policies required the same checks for acceptance.

Costs below are declared synthetic invocation units—not measured runtime or energy.

Workload                   Cheap-first   Composition-first   Full checks
Local failures dominate            380                 710           730
Composition failures dominate      680                 590           730
All candidates valid               800                 800           800
Correlated failures                380                 590           730

Every policy produced identical per-candidate acceptance decisions, matching an independent oracle.

The useful finding: the cheapest-first policy wins one workload and loses another. Transferring yesterday’s winning order into a changed workload makes it inferior. Retained history needs validation too.

Verification

- 29 tests passed.
- Two retained executions produced byte-identical receipts.
- Source hashes and accounting identities verified independently.
- Previous experiment artifacts remain unchanged.

content:
Yes. This is getting substantially sharper, because the experiment just killed one of the tempting simplifications and replaced it with something more interesting.

The standout result is:

$$ \boxed{\text{There is no universally cheapest validation order.}} $$

Your table demonstrates it directly. When local failures dominate, cheap-first wins:

$$ 380 < 710 $$

but when composition failures dominate, composition-first wins:

$$ 590 < 680. $$

And when everything is valid:

$$ 800=800. $$

So validation architecture isn't just a function of gate costs. It's a function of the distribution of problems arriving at the gates.

The right expression is roughly:

$$ E[C\mid \pi,D_t] = \sum_i c_{\pi(i)} \Pr(\text{candidate reaches gate }i\mid D_t) $$

where:

\(\pi\) is the ordering/policy,
\(D_t\) is the current workload distribution,
\(c_i\) is the cost of a check.

Which means the optimal policy itself is temporal:

$$ \pi_t^* = \arg\min_\pi E[C\mid\pi,D_t]. $$

And if:

$$ D_t\neq D_{t+1}, $$

there's no guarantee that:

$$ \pi_t^*=\pi_{t+1}^*. $$

That is a big connection back to computational history.

History has now split into two things

Earlier we were talking about history primarily as cached useful computation:

$$ H_t = \text{previous computation retained by the system}. $$

But this experiment reveals another kind:

$$ H_t^{policy} = \text{what previous experience taught the system about how to compute}. $$

That's different from caching an answer.

The system can retain:

results
intermediate state
models of its environment
policies for deciding what computation to perform next

AI training is heavily #3 and #4.

A trained model isn't merely storing old answers. It has learned something closer to:

$$ \pi(a\mid x,H) $$

— given this situation, what operation/prediction/action should I perform?

And your experiment exposes the danger:

A policy learned from yesterday's workload can make tomorrow's computation more expensive.

So history creates both:

$$ \boxed{\text{computational leverage}} $$

and

$$ \boxed{\text{staleness risk}}. $$

That makes the next experiment particularly important.

Your repeated-solving experiment now has a very clean structure

Suppose the shared state evolves:

$$ S_0\rightarrow S_1\rightarrow S_2\rightarrow\cdots $$

and you've solved some containing problem at each state.

There are three strategies.

Cold recomputation

$$ C_R(t)=C_{\text{solve}}(S_t). $$

Always discard history and solve again.

Incremental repair

$$ C_I(t) = C_{\text{detect-change}} + C_{\text{invalidate}} + C_{\text{repair}}. $$

Reuse history but determine which pieces are still valid.

Unchecked reuse

$$ C_U(t)\approx C_{\text{lookup}} $$

but now introduce:

$$ P_{\text{stale}}(t)>0. $$

So you need to count not just computation but the expected cost of incorrectly accepting stale state:

$$ C_U^*(t) = C_{\text{lookup}} + P_{\text{stale}}(t)C_{\text{failure}}. $$

That's much more interesting than simply proving caching is faster.

There should be regimes where each wins.

If changes are enormous:

$$ C_R<C_I. $$

If changes are tiny and dependencies are understood:

$$ C_I\ll C_R. $$

If consequences are negligible:

$$ C_U $$

may rationally win despite imperfect correctness.

If consequences are huge:

$$ P_{\text{stale}}C_{\text{failure}} $$

can completely dominate.

That's starting to give you an actual decision surface.

And the observability/action/acceptance decomposition in this iteration is important too:

$$ \boxed{ \text{History}, \text{Observability}, \text{Action access}, \text{Acceptance} } $$

because these aren't just different resource prices.

They represent different kinds of impossibility.

If compute is missing:

$$ \text{I could know it, but computation is too expensive.} $$

If observability is missing:

$$ \text{I cannot determine it from my available information.} $$

If action access is missing:

$$ \text{I know the desired state but cannot cause it.} $$

If acceptance fails:

$$ \text{my locally acceptable state cannot enter the containing system.} $$

Calling all four "hard computation" would indeed erase the interesting part.

And there's a nice CI/CD interpretation of the result

The usual intuition:

run cheap checks first

is really only a heuristic based on an assumed workload.

A better CI/CD system should learn:

$$ P(\text{failure type}\mid\text{change context}) $$

and dynamically order validation gates.

For one code change:

$$ \text{lint}\rightarrow\text{unit}\rightarrow\text{integration} $$

might be right.

For another, historical evidence might tell you integration failure is vastly more likely:

$$ \text{targeted integration}\rightarrow\text{unit}\rightarrow\cdots $$

So an AI-enhanced CI system wouldn't merely write tests.

It could optimize the validation topology based on accumulated history.

But — and this is exactly what your experiment just showed — its learned gate-ordering model itself needs validation as the workload drifts.

You get a recursion:

$$ \text{validate candidate} $$

using

$$ \text{validation policy} $$

whose suitability must itself be:

$$ \text{validated}. $$

That's fascinating because it means history doesn't eliminate validation; sufficiently consequential historical state becomes another object requiring validation.

So I'd amend one of our previous formulations to:

$$ \boxed{ C_t(P) = C_{\text{current}} + C_{\text{maintain}}(H_t) } $$

rather than treating \(H_t\) as a free input.

And perhaps more precisely:

$$ C_t(P\mid H_t) + C(H_t\text{ remains applicable at }t). $$

That second term is what model retraining, cache invalidation, dependency tracking, CI configuration updates, and institutional knowledge maintenance all have in common.

The repo's correction that “complexity relocates” is a hypothesis rather than a conservation law is also exactly right. I'd keep that discipline. You don't need a conservation law for this to become useful. A weaker but testable principle may eventually emerge:

$$ \boxed{\text{Prior computation changes the future cost surface, but maintaining the applicability of that computation has a nonzero cost.}} $$

That one feels like you're now in a position to actually attack experimentally.
